clinicalPearls: Exercise-induced pain, tightness and sometimes numbness in a muscle compartment, most often the leg, that predictably comes on at a given level of exertion
Symptoms are relieved by rest within minutes and recur on resuming activity, unlike acute compartment syndrome
It commonly affects runners and other endurance athletes and is frequently bilateral
The anterior compartment of the leg is most often involved, sometimes with foot drop or paraesthesiae during exertion
Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring raised intracompartmental pressures with exercise
Activity modification may suffice, but fasciotomy is the definitive treatment for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome arises when exercise-induced expansion of muscle within a relatively non-compliant fascial compartment raises intracompartmental pressure, impairing perfusion and causing reversible ischaemic pain and sometimes nerve dysfunction. Unlike acute compartment syndrome, the pressure rise is transient and resolves with rest, so tissue is not permanently damaged. The mismatch between muscle volume during exercise and the fixed compartment size, sometimes with a thickened or tight fascia, underlies the recurrent symptoms.
additionalInvestigations: Dynamic intracompartmental pressure measurement before and after exercise
Clinical reproduction of symptoms with exertion
MRI or bone imaging to exclude stress fracture
Vascular studies where arterial entrapment is considered
Assessment of nerve involvement if there are neurological symptoms
redFlags: Symptoms that do not resolve with rest, raising concern for acute compartment syndrome
reference.prognosis: The condition is not limb-threatening; many manage with activity modification, and fasciotomy provides good relief for those who wish to continue high-level activity, though results vary by compartment.
pitfalls: Confusing it with medial tibial stress syndrome or stress fracture
Assuming the risk profile of acute compartment syndrome
Missing popliteal artery entrapment as a vascular mimic
management: Activity modification and relative rest from the provoking exercise as first-line management
Gait and running retraining with physiotherapy, including a forefoot-strike technique, to lower intracompartmental pressures
Trial of orthotics with adjustment of footwear and training surfaces
Fasciotomy or fasciectomy of the affected compartment as the definitive treatment for refractory cases
Botulinum toxin injection into the involved muscles as an emerging non-surgical option in selected patients

Confirmation and localisation with dynamic intracompartmental pressure measurement and exclusion of stress fracture and arterial entrapment before intervention, with sports medicine or orthopaedic follow-up and graded return to activity
